intervals.label: operating as a civilian underground laboratory (earliest dated use found)
intervals.locator: arXiv:astro-ph/0001511, Sec. on the SIMPLE installation
intervals.note: Earliest dated scientific use found, not a founding or opening date: the SIMPLE paper says the installation of detector modules 500 m underground started in July 1999 in the converted missile control centre, and the October 1999 characterisation paper (arXiv:astro-ph/9910192) reports the site as already converted; a radon measurement in the capsule dates from January 1998 (same paper). No source read gives the date of the conversion or of the laboratory's creation. The official site shows the laboratory still active in 2026 (news items for September to October 2026).
intervals.quote: started in July 1999. A decommissioned nuclear missile control center has been converted into an underground laboratory

name: Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit
notes: Military origin (official history page, lsbb.eu/histoire): the strategic missile system of the Plateau d'Albion was in permanent operation from August 1971 to September 1996 and was dismantled in 1996; the LSBB comes from the reconversion of one of the two fire-control posts. The conversion date is not given in any source read.

Name: 'Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit' is the name on the laboratory's own website; the 1999 paper writes 'Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit de Rustrel-Pays d'Apt', and later papers translate it as Low Noise Underground Laboratory. Depth and overburden are on the site record.
The unit's supervisory bodies changed over time: SIMPLE papers of 2014 give 'UMS 3538 UNS/UAPV/CNRS'; the official site now gives 'UAR 3538' with CNRS and Avignon Université.

summary.plain: A low-noise underground laboratory at Rustrel in southern France, made from a former underground missile control centre. About 500 m of rock shields it from cosmic rays, and it hosted the SIMPLE dark matter search.
summary.technical: Laboratoire Souterrain à Bas Bruit (LSBB), a CNRS / Avignon Université research support unit (UAR 3538) at Rustrel (Vaucluse), converted from one of the two former fire-control posts of the French strategic missile system on the Plateau d'Albion. The deepest experimental hall lies under 500 m of calcite rock (about 1500 m.w.e.) and holds a 100 m^2 floor on shock absorbers inside a steel Faraday cage; the GESA cavern used by SIMPLE is at 505 m depth.
